title: Upper-canopy chlorosis
scenario: A plant develops pale new leaves near the top while older leaves remain noticeably greener. The grower is tempted to add more micronutrients immediately.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Newest leaves and upper growing points

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Pale tissue with veins remaining somewhat more visible

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Appeared first on recent growth

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: No root-zone pH or EC measurement has been taken yet

question: What is the strongest next step before changing the nutrient recipe?

options.label: Add a concentrated micronutrient supplement immediately
options.rationale: Appearance alone does not establish whether a nutrient is absent, unavailable, or whether root function is limiting uptake.

options.label: Measure root-zone pH and EC with a consistent method
options.rationale: This directly tests whether chemical availability or salt concentration could explain why young tissue is affected before changing inputs.

options.label: Remove every pale leaf and wait for replacement growth
options.rationale: Removing evidence does not identify the process driving the pattern and can make progression harder to track.

options.label: Increase irrigation frequency without measuring the root zone
options.rationale: More water can worsen some root-zone problems and does not test the leading competing explanations.

differential: Root stress limiting uptake even when nutrients are present
A true micronutrient shortage in the supplied solution
takeaway: Young-growth chlorosis narrows the field, but location does not prove a nutrient deficiency. Measure the root-zone context before changing the formula.

title: Lower-leaf yellowing
scenario: Several older lower leaves are becoming uniformly yellow while the newest growth remains green. The change has progressed upward slowly over several days.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Oldest leaves first

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Mostly uniform yellowing rather than isolated spots

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Slowly moving upward from the lower canopy

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: No recent record of input EC, root-zone EC, or feeding trend

question: Which observation would most improve the differential?

options.label: Only compare the leaf to an online deficiency photo
options.rationale: Photo matching ignores progression, plant stage, root-zone chemistry, and several causes that can create similar yellowing.

options.label: Record input and root-zone EC together with the recent feeding trend
options.rationale: That adds context about nutrient supply and accumulation while preserving the useful clue that older tissue is affected first.

options.label: Increase every nutrient because the leaf is yellow
options.rationale: A broad increase can compound excess salts and does not distinguish shortage from uptake or root-zone problems.

options.label: Ignore which leaves were affected first
options.rationale: Tissue age and progression are among the most useful observations for separating competing explanations.

differential: Remobilization of a mobile nutrient from older tissue
Insufficient nutrient supply relative to plant demand
takeaway: Older-leaf-first symptoms are valuable because mobile resources can be remobilized, but the feeding and root-zone record is still needed before deciding why it is happening.

title: Tip burn after a feed change
scenario: Leaf tips begin browning across multiple parts of the canopy shortly after the nutrient concentration was increased. New growth is still expanding.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Tips on leaves across several canopy levels

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Small necrotic tips with otherwise intact leaf blades

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Began after a known increase in feed strength

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: Root-zone EC has not been checked since the change

question: What measurement best tests the strongest timeline-based hypothesis?

options.label: Measure root-zone EC and compare it with the input EC
options.rationale: The timing makes salt concentration or accumulation a plausible explanation, and the input/root-zone comparison directly tests it.

options.label: Add another supplement to cover possible deficiencies
options.rationale: Adding more dissolved salts before checking EC can worsen the very condition suggested by the timeline.

options.label: Judge the entire root zone from one damaged leaf tip
options.rationale: The tip is evidence of stress, not a direct measurement of the root-zone cause.

options.label: Change the light schedule because the tips are brown
options.rationale: Nothing in the current timeline specifically points to photoperiod as the best discriminating variable.

differential: Elevated root-zone EC after the feed increase
A separate environmental stress coinciding with the feed change
takeaway: A strong timeline clue should shape the next measurement. When symptoms follow a feed-strength change, compare input and root-zone EC before adding more nutrients.

title: Droop after irrigation
scenario: A plant repeatedly droops soon after irrigation. The medium remains wet for a long time and the plant improves only after the root zone has dried somewhat.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Whole plant rather than one branch

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Leaves and petioles lose posture without a localized lesion

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Consistently follows irrigation events

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: Long wet periods and slow dryback

question: Which next check best separates water shortage from a saturated root-zone problem?

options.label: Irrigate again immediately because the plant is drooping
options.rationale: The timing and long wet period make additional water a poor test and potentially a worsening factor.

options.label: Measure root-zone moisture/dryback and inspect drainage/aeration
options.rationale: This tests whether the roots are remaining saturated and whether oxygen availability or drainage is limiting root function.

options.label: Diagnose a nutrient deficiency from droop alone
options.rationale: Loss of posture is nonspecific and must be interpreted with water status, timing, and root-zone conditions.

options.label: Remove healthy leaves to reduce the visible droop
options.rationale: Removing tissue does not identify whether the root system is short of water or short of oxygen.

differential: Saturated root zone reducing oxygen availability
Poor drainage or insufficient air-filled porosity
Less likely true water shortage given the repeated post-irrigation timing
takeaway: Droop is not synonymous with thirst. Timing relative to irrigation and the root zone's wet/dry cycle can reverse the interpretation.

title: Midday upper-leaf curl
scenario: Upper leaves curl upward most strongly during the brightest, warmest part of the light cycle and relax later. Lower leaves show much less of the effect.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Upper canopy closest to the light

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Upward edge curl without the same severity below

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Strongest during peak light/heat and partially reversible

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: No leaf-temperature, PPFD, or canopy RH readings have been compared yet

question: Which measurement set best tests the spatial and time-of-day pattern?

options.label: Leaf temperature, PPFD, RH/VPD, and light distance at the affected canopy
options.rationale: These measurements directly test the microclimate variables that change with canopy height and time of day.

options.label: Only the nutrient bottle label
options.rationale: The label cannot explain why symptoms are strongest near the light and vary through the day.

options.label: Only the room temperature measured far from the canopy
options.rationale: A distant air reading can miss leaf temperature and the microclimate actually experienced by the affected tissue.

options.label: Immediately raise nutrient EC
options.rationale: The spatial and reversible pattern points first toward canopy environment, not a reason to increase dissolved salts.

differential: Excess leaf temperature or radiant load at the upper canopy
High evaporative demand relative to water delivery
Airflow or boundary-layer differences near the affected leaves
takeaway: A symptom that tracks canopy position and time of day should be investigated as a microclimate problem before it is treated as a nutrient problem.

title: One branch wilts while the rest looks normal
scenario: One branch loses posture and slows while the rest of the plant remains vigorous. The grower is considering changing the nutrient mix for the whole plant.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: One branch and its attached leaves

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Localized rather than distributed through the canopy

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: The affected branch worsens while neighboring branches remain normal

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: The branch junction and local stem have not been inspected closely

question: What should be inspected before changing whole-plant nutrition?

options.label: The branch junction, stem tissue, and local vascular continuity
options.rationale: A one-branch pattern strongly supports checking for a localized structural or transport problem before changing systemic nutrition.

options.label: Increase fertilizer for the entire root zone
options.rationale: A whole-plant nutrient change is poorly matched to a symptom confined to one branch.

options.label: Assume every leaf on the plant has the same problem
options.rationale: Spatial distribution is evidence; ignoring it removes one of the strongest clues in the case.

options.label: Change the photoperiod immediately
options.rationale: Photoperiod is a whole-plant variable and does not explain why only one branch is affected.

differential: Localized stem or branch damage affecting transport
A localized biological injury rather than a systemic nutrient problem
takeaway: Localized symptoms deserve localized inspection. Distribution across the plant often tells you whether to investigate a whole-system variable or a specific structure.
